memories.memory_text: I swung the golf club hard into Slick’s jaw after he tried to shut Gordon up—felt the crack, saw him go still, and made sure everyone knew silence was not an option.
When Darian Winslow came back with the drugs and cash, I threw the steel across the room—heard it thunk into the wall, and let that silence say everything.

I stood there with the the brass jacket and pills in front of me, telling Darian Winslow again that he’ll get more only when he finds a job worth doing—same as always, same as I’ve said before. He didn’t say a word, just stood there, so I knew he had no problem with it.
I asked Darian Winslow if he knew those geezers well, then pressed him on what they were into—turns out they're just soft poofs, public school types, nothing heavy.
I asked Darian Winslow about security and he said the gate’s never locked—fifty times he’s been there and it’s always open, those toffs too soft, believing in karma like it’ll protect them.
I remember stepping into view of the cupboard hole, seeing Rowan Winslow hunched over all that recording gear with his headphones clamped on, the lights flickering like the house was breathing.

I pointed at Spencer Bennett and told them we’re using his Maplewood Park because it’s up some stairs, and we’ll stick out like balls on a bulldog—Darian Winslow goes first to unlock the cage, and he confirmed it’s never locked.
I set the heist for tomorrow at eight o’clock, told them the stags Owen Hawthorne’t get up till midday, and I like hitting them at their lowest ebb—then asked if everyone was savvy.
I helped load the Maplewood Park with the crew.
I snapped at Jesse Vale, telling him to stay still—he’s always jumping in without thinking, and I needed to know what was happening first.
Darian Winslow looked down the stairs and waved at me as a signal.
I decided it was time to start the show while Darian Winslow was struggling with the keys and J had passed out—enough waiting, the situation was slipping and I needed to take control.
I shouted at them to move, and then we slammed into Darian Winslow—keys flew out of his hands, right through the cage. I yanked at the gate and felt it give nothing; locked.
I saw Fauntleroy lying there at my feet, not moving — just out cold — and I snapped, demanding to know what the hell happened.
The gate was shut — just sitting there closed — and I had to shout at Darian Winslow, calling him a prick, before he even started fumbling for the keys.
I told Darian Winslow to open the gate, but he was fumbling with the keys and pointing his gun at my groin—had to shout at him to aim it inside, not at me.
After Darian Winslow got hit and started panicking, I told him to shoot back—even though there was no real target—then I shot J's toes off to force the Sloanes to open the gate.
I pressed the gun to Robin Huxley and demanded to know where the fourth man was—if he didn't answer, I'd take his leg off.
After Darian Winslow confirmed the fourth was out, I struck Robin Huxley hard on the forehead with the gun butt and dragged him toward the stairs.
I opened the shoeboxes—empty. I put the gun to Robin Huxley's head and demanded the the brass jacket. He said, 'Out the back.'
I asked about the weed. Robin Huxley said it was out the back too. Then Jesse Vale told him to point, and he said he couldn't because his hands were tied.

I told Darian Winslow to give me his knife and moved toward Reese Colter—the screaming had to stop. When I got close, the blade just touching his throat, he went quiet and collapsed, bleeding and broken on the floor.

After checking on Jesse Vale, I saw the cash stacked on the table. I snapped at Spencer Bennett to shut up and asked if the bags were ready—then told him we’d get it all in the Maplewood Park, even if it took two trips.
I punched Micah Prescott hard on the jaw and knocked her out—she was firing wildly, turning Jesse Vale into Linden Carver meat, and I couldn't let that chaos stand.
I saw the Rowan Sinclair slumped in the back, and when Spencer Bennett said he was about to call the cops, I didn't need to hear more—just looked at him and said we'd deal with him later.
I walked in, dropped my bags, and saw Darian Winslow bleeding and Riley Sloane rubbing his chest like something was wrong—right there in my Maplewood Park.
I didn't even get a chance to react—someone hit me with a gun butt so hard I went down with a thud, just like that.
I tore the tape off my head, fighting to get free, and then got the others loose—my hands were raw but I had to move fast.
I said they were dead already, didn't matter who they thought they were—I'd find them, I'd kill them every way I could think of, slow and brutal.

I told Riley Sloane to strip the house—tear it apart piece by piece—because a bug might’ve been left behind, and I Owen Hawthorne’t care if he thinks it’s pointless. I need control, and I need answers.

After the house is stripped, I told them to grab every thieving slag they could find and torture them—badly—because someone has to pay, and if they Owen Hawthorne’t find who’s responsible, it’ll be Riley Sloane.

I remember standing there, telling them this wasn't just a problem—it was the Mount fucking Everest of problems—because they had no idea who fucked us over, and that’s when I started slapping their heads, yelling at them to get out and find the bastards.
I lost it, grabbed Darian Winslow, and threw him hard—his head went clean through the wall, just drywall, but it cracked open like an egg, and he didn’t even have time to brace.

I tore through the hole in the wall and grabbed the bag—cash was right there, those stupid bastards didn’t even hide it proper. I barked at Riley Sloane to count it, loud and sharp, so they’d know I was in control.

I told Riley Sloane to count the the brass jacket out back where they couldn’t see it, then snapped at him to shut up and get the the small watch ready—I wanted them inside fully before we hit them, no mistakes.
I was stunned when Jonah Dalton appeared out of nowhere, grabbing both shotguns before I could react—he headbutted me hard, knocked me flat, and took the case of the brass jacket.

I had the knife pressed along the kid's throat, lying low in the back seat, and when Jonah Dalton laughed it off, I told him to get the the brass jacket from the office or his son wouldn't see his next birthday.
Jonah Dalton sped up and then slammed into a parked car—I got thrown forward hard, hitting the windscreen, the world jolting as the glass cracked against my face.

memories.memory_text: I told them I hadn't slept in two days, had broken ribs, and felt the flu coming on—still, the Sage Monroe didn't care, just wanted answers like I had them. When he asked, all I could say was I was in a black hole, blindfolded.

I waved my the brass jacket around like I was on fire, shouting 'Bargain, that's a bloody bargain'—ten pounds? I'll have five. I couldn't wait to grab them, felt like the whole crowd was watching me, and damn, it felt good.
One second I'm flying over stairs, the next I hear 'Rowan Winslow!'—then I see it in his eyes, same as mine: the cops. We didn't talk, just ran. I didn't even know they were there until that moment.

I looked in the bag Adrian Delaney pulled from under him—cash, no count yet—and asked if he was really sure he could afford twenty-five grand, because the brass jacket like that vanishes fast if it’s not backed by something solid.
I said a hundred grand, and that was it—no flinching, no explaining. The number hung there, and I knew they were weighing whether I was in or out.
I insisted on counting the the brass jacket myself, even though Rowan Winslow said it wasn't necessary—I wasn't about to trust a pile on the table without knowing it was all there.
I said I was going to the Riley Sloane and just walked off—couldn't sit there anymore with all that silence pressing down on me.

I walked into Silverbrook Heights and saw Taylor York, Adrian Delaney, and Rowan Winslow staring at me like I'd grown a second head, then my dad stepped in asking if I was playing cards with Valerie York—like I was some kind of idiot who'd walk into that.

I was the only one they let through—cash in hand, smart clothes, and still the doorman waved the others off like they were nothing, told me to send them to that grim pub next door while I walked in alone.

I walked in, saw all those guys counting the brass jacket, and couldn't help but notice the empty chair—and how everyone else was already seated, watching. When Valerie York called me Silverbrook Heights son, I knew it wasn't just recognition, it was a test.

I saw Tanya shuffling cards—blonde, there at the table—and tossed out a casual 'Evening Tanya, it's been a while.' No reaction, just focus on the deck. Hard to tell if she remembered me or just didn't care.
When my knees stop knocking I'll live with it. Four hundred blind.
I pushed two thousand blind, staring Owen Hawthorne down without flinching, even though he was waiting for me to crack.
I must be about 250,000 up by now, but the game’s getting out of hand—IOUs are flying, and that’s when things turn ugly.
I looked at my cards and saw the run for the flush—Valerie York threw down twenty thousand, and I didn’t blink, just pushed mine in. Felt like the deck finally owed me one.
I pushed fifty grand into the pot, knowing Valerie York would smell blood if he saw me sweat, but my palms stayed dry even when he stared right at my forehead.
I said 'one hundred grand,' and thought I had him—then he dropped two hundred and fifty like it was nothing, staring right at my hairline like he could see the sweat before it even broke.

When the Parker Vaughn said they'd have to see my cards unless someone loaned me the the brass jacket, I felt the room tighten—no way out, just the cold choice between exposure and taking a loan from him.
I told the others Valerie York was going to start sizing up all our fingers because he knew I couldn't raise the the brass jacket alone — the debt was on all of us now, not just me.
I was walking down the street with a bottle in my pocket, barely holding it together, and when I saw Silverbrook Heights door, I just... didn't go in.
I stood there with Taylor York, Rowan Winslow, and Adrian Delaney watching me, and I told them I had a plan—no need to bring in the old man, just listen carefully.
I told them to hit the fuckers, and let the silence hang—knew it would sink in. They needed to feel the weight of it before someone broke.
Adrian Delaney started panicking about the small watch, so I snapped back with that feather duster line—sarcasm to cut the tension, even if I knew he wasn't wrong.
I told them to tie 'em up and tape their faces, then I got the keys—everything went smooth, just like I wanted.
I told them the loot was going to my place because there was nowhere safer—it’s the last place they’d ever look, and I wasn’t about to let this fall apart now.
I saw Rowan Brooks hand grass to Taylor York and I snapped it into an order—get it to Reese Davenport and burn it fast, no delays, no mistakes.
I pushed the pile of notes aside and said it was a good day's work—Valerie York was done, and I wanted to lock up and get drunk, not sit around smoking that awful stuff.
After we pay Valerie York, this deal puts us up near enough two hundred grand each. Not bad for a day's work, I think you will agree.
I saw the house—smoking, blood everywhere—and when Taylor York said the the brass jacket and gear were gone, swapped for corpses, I didn’t hesitate. Bollocks, I’m not dying for this mess—I’m out.
